blocks.text: A hypervisor runs multiple virtual machines, each with its own guest OS and kernel, on shared hardware. Type 1 runs directly on the hardware; Type 2 runs as an application on a host OS.

rows: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, KVM (kernel module turning Linux into a hypervisor)

blocks.src: generate: Two stacks side by side: Type 1 (hardware → hypervisor → VMs with guest OS + apps) and Type 2 (hardware → host OS → hypervisor app → VMs with guest OS + apps)
blocks.caption: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisors.

items: Hardware-assisted virtualization (Intel VT-x, AMD-V, mid-2000s) lets guest kernels run with CPU support instead of slow binary translation.
Paravirtualized drivers (virtio) speed up disk and network I/O.
Each VM gets virtual CPUs, memory, disks and NICs, and boots a full OS.

blocks.text: The line blurs: KVM is a Linux kernel module (Type 1 behavior on a general-purpose OS), and Docker Desktop runs a lightweight Linux VM on macOS/Windows to host containers.

Q: "Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?" A: "Type 1 runs directly on hardware (ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen, KVM) and is used in data centers and clouds; Type 2 runs on top of a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) for desktops. Either way each VM has its own kernel, unlike containers, which share the host kernel."

items: VMs virtualize hardware; each has its own kernel.
Type 1 = on hardware; Type 2 = on a host OS.
Public clouds are built on Type 1 hypervisors.
